how_to_obtain.instruction: Retrieve a sample of recent registry audit log entries and inspect the fields present in each record.
how_to_obtain.command: tail -20 /var/log/registry/access.log | python3 -c "import sys, json; [print(json.dumps(list(json.loads(l).keys()), indent=2)) for l in sys.stdin if l.strip()]"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each log entry's key list should contain fields mapping to 'timestamp' (or 'time'/'@timestamp'), 'client_identity' (or 'username'/'auth.user.name'), and 'image_reference' (or 'request.url'/'repository'). Missing keys identify absent fields.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For AWS ECR via CloudTrail, inspect a sample CloudTrail event to verify the fields present for an ECR API call.
how_to_obtain.command: aws cloudtrail lookup-events --lookup-attributes AttributeKey=EventSource,AttributeValue=ecr.amazonaws.com --max-results 1 --output json | jq '.Events[0].CloudTrailEvent | fromjson | {eventTime, userIdentity: .userIdentity.arn, requestParameters}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'eventTime' maps to timestamp, 'userIdentity.arn' maps to client_identity, and 'requestParameters' (containing repositoryName and imageIds) maps to image_reference. All three should be non-null.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Harbor, inspect a single audit log entry via the API to enumerate its fields.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -u admin:<password> 'https://<harbor-host>/api/v2.0/audit-logs?page_size=1' | jq '.[0] | keys'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Keys should include 'op_time' (timestamp), 'username' (client_identity), and 'resource' (image_reference). The 'resource_type' field should confirm the scope is 'artifact'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For self-hosted registries with custom log formatters, review the log format template to identify which fields are templated into each entry.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -E '(format|template|fields)' /etc/docker/registry/config.yml /etc/harbor/harbor.yml 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Log format configuration should reference time/timestamp, user/identity, and repository/image variables. Absence of these references means the fields are not emitted.

option_description: Controls whether the registry enforces a policy that prevents any client from overwriting an existing image tag with a new image digest — ensuring that once a tag like 'v1.2.3' is published and points to a specific SHA256 digest, no subsequent push can silently replace the referenced image.
security_impact: The Rego rule `tag_mutability_without_immutability_enforcement` fires when `tag_immutability_enabled` is false and either mutable tags are in active use or push permissions are broad (team_wide/organization_wide). Without immutability, an authorized push client (or a compromised CI/CD pipeline credential) can overwrite any tag, silently replacing a known-good production image with a malicious one — a supply-chain poisoning vector that maps to MITRE T1525 (Implant Internal Image), T1204.003 (Malicious Image), and T1601.001 (Patch System Image). The attack is particularly insidious because orchestration manifests referencing the overwritten tag will pull the malicious image without any visible configuration change.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For AWS ECR, retrieve the image tag mutability setting for each repository.
how_to_obtain.command: aws ecr describe-repositories --region <region> --output json | jq '.repositories[] | {repositoryName, imageTagMutability}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'imageTagMutability' should be 'IMMUTABLE' for all production repositories. A value of 'MUTABLE' indicates immutability is not enforced.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Harbor, check the project-level immutable tag rules via the Harbor API.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -u admin:<password> 'https://<harbor-host>/api/v2.0/projects/<project-id>/immutabletagrules' | jq 'length, .'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A non-empty array of immutable tag rules indicates the feature is configured. An empty array '[]' or length of 0 means no immutability rules are in place.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Harbor, inspect immutable tag rules through the UI.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Harbor UI → <Project> → Policy → Immutable Tags. Review the list of configured rules. Rules matching 'all images, all tags' or specific production tag patterns indicate enforcement is active.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: At least one enabled immutable tag rule is present. An empty rules list or all rules disabled means tag immutability is not enforced.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For JFrog Artifactory, query the repository configuration for the forceDockerTagImmutability property.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -u <user>:<password> 'https://<artifactory-host>/artifactory/api/repositories/<repo-key>' | jq '.dockerApiVersion, .forceDockerTagImmutability'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'forceDockerTagImmutability' should be 'true'. A value of 'false' or the field being absent indicates tags are mutable.

option_description: Enumerates the set of non-digest image tag names (e.g., 'latest', 'stable', 'production', 'release') that are actively referenced in Kubernetes manifests, Helm values files, or CI/CD pipeline definitions and that can be silently overwritten to point to a different image digest.
security_impact: The Rego rule `tag_mutability_without_immutability_enforcement` fires when `tag_immutability_enabled` is false and `count(mutable_tags_in_use) > 0`. Mutable tags amplify the impact of absent immutability enforcement: each mutable tag in active use in orchestration manifests is a live attack surface where a supply-chain poisoning push immediately affects production workloads. Tags like 'latest' and 'stable' are particularly dangerous because they are common knowledge, frequently targeted, and their overwrite goes undetected without image digest pinning. This maps to MITRE T1525 and T1204.003.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Scan all Kubernetes manifests in the cluster for image references that do not use digest pinning.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get pods,deployments,statefulsets,daemonsets,cronjobs --all-namespaces -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{range .spec.template.spec.containers[*]}{.image}{"\n"}{end}{end}' | grep -v '@sha256:' | grep -oP '(?<=:)[^:@]+$' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each line shows a count and a tag name. Tags like 'latest', 'stable', 'production', 'main', 'release' appearing in this list confirm mutable tags are in active use. Only sha256 digests would be safe.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Search Helm values files and CI/CD pipeline definitions for mutable tag patterns.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -rE 'image:.*:(latest|stable|production|release|main|master|dev|staging)([^a-zA-Z0-9]|$)' --include='*.yaml' --include='*.yml' --include='*.json' . | grep -v '@sha256:'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: File paths and line content showing image references with non-digest tags. Each match represents a mutable tag in active use. Zero matches indicate all references are digest-pinned.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the container registry API to list tags for high-value repositories and identify commonly used mutable tag names.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' 'https://<registry-host>/v2/<repository>/tags/list' | jq '.tags | map(select(test("^(latest|stable|production|release|main|dev|staging)$")))'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Array of mutable tag names that exist in the repository. These should be cross-referenced with manifest references to confirm active use.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect CI/CD pipeline configuration files for hardcoded mutable image tag references.
how_to_obtain.command: find . -name '*.gitlab-ci.yml' -o -name 'Jenkinsfile' -o -name '*.github/workflows/*.yml' 2>/dev/null | xargs grep -hE 'image:.*:' | grep -vE '@sha256:[a-f0-9]{64}' | sort | uniq
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lines containing image references with tag names rather than digests. Each unique non-digest tag found in pipeline files represents a mutable tag in use.

option_description: Controls whether the registry runs an automated garbage collection (GC) process on a schedule to identify and delete unreferenced blob objects — image layer tarballs and manifests that are no longer pointed to by any tag or manifest list — reclaiming storage and eliminating orphaned data.
security_impact: The Rego rule `missing_garbage_collection_and_retention_policy` fires when `garbage_collection_enabled` is false (regardless of whether a retention policy exists, and also when only one of the two controls is present). Without GC, deleted or superseded image layers remain physically present in the storage backend indefinitely. These orphaned blobs may contain secrets, proprietary code, or vulnerable dependency versions from images that were intentionally removed. An adversary with storage-layer access can exfiltrate this data via MITRE T1530 (Data from Cloud Storage), and the absence of lifecycle controls corresponds to MITRE T1485.001 (Lifecycle-Triggered Deletion). The finding is scored 2 (low criticality) but compounds other storage exposure risks significantly.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For AWS ECR, check whether lifecycle policies are configured (ECR uses lifecycle policies rather than a separate GC process).
how_to_obtain.command: aws ecr describe-repositories --region <region> --output json | jq '.repositories[].repositoryName' | xargs -I{} aws ecr get-lifecycle-policy --repository-name {} --region <region> 2>&1 | grep -v LifecyclePolicyNotFoundException
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Valid JSON lifecycle policy output for each repository indicates GC-equivalent automation is configured. 'LifecyclePolicyNotFoundException' for any repository means GC is absent for that repository.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For self-hosted Docker Distribution (registry:2), check the storage configuration for a maintenance/GC cron job or startup flag.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -A 5 'maintenance:' /etc/docker/registry/config.yml && crontab -l | grep -i 'registry garbage-collect\|registry gc'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: The maintenance section should show 'uploadpurging: { enabled: true }'. A crontab entry invoking 'registry garbage-collect /etc/docker/registry/config.yml' confirms automated GC. Absence of both indicates GC is not configured.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Harbor, verify garbage collection schedule configuration in the admin panel.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Harbor UI → Administration → Garbage Collection. Review the 'Schedule' field — it should show a cron expression or 'Daily'/'Weekly' preset. The 'Last GC Time' field should show a recent timestamp confirming the job has run.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A non-empty schedule is configured and 'Last GC Time' is within the expected interval (e.g., within the past 7 days for weekly schedules). 'None' schedule means GC is disabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Harbor, query the GC schedule and history via the Harbor API.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -u admin:<password> 'https://<harbor-host>/api/v2.0/system/gc/schedule' | jq '{schedule: .schedule, next_scheduled_time: .next_scheduled_time} ' && curl -s -u admin:<password> 'https://<harbor-host>/api/v2.0/system/gc?page_size=5' | jq '[.[] | {id, creation_time, job_status}]'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Schedule object should have a 'type' of 'Daily', 'Weekly', or 'Custom' with a valid cron string — not 'None'. GC history should show recent successful ('Success') job runs.

option_description: Controls whether an automated image retention policy is active that expires and removes old, untagged, or excess images and their layer blobs from the registry after a defined time period or count threshold. This directly governs whether stale image data accumulates indefinitely on backend storage.
security_impact: The Rego rule missing_garbage_collection_and_retention_policy fires when retention_policy_configured is false (or absent) regardless of garbage collection state, and also fires when garbage_collection_enabled is true but retention_policy_configured is false. Without a retention policy, unreferenced blobs containing deleted but sensitive layer data persist indefinitely, expanding the exfiltration surface. Orphaned layers embedded with secrets, credentials, or proprietary code remain accessible to any actor with storage-layer access even after the manifest is deleted.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Harbor: navigate to Projects → [Project Name] → Policy → Tag Retention. Check whether any retention rules are listed and enabled. For ECR: open the AWS Console, go to ECR → Repositories → [Repository] → Lifecycle Policy and verify at least one rule exists. For GCR/Artifact Registry: navigate to Artifact Registry → [Repository] → Settings and inspect Cleanup Policies.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Harbor: Projects → [Project] → Policy → Tag Retention | ECR: ECR → Repositories → [Repo] → Lifecycle Policy | GCR: Artifact Registry → [Repo] → Settings → Cleanup Policies
how_to_obtain.expected_output: At least one active retention rule specifying a maximum image count or maximum age is present.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Harbor, query the retention policy API for a project. For ECR, describe the lifecycle policy. For GCR/Artifact Registry, list cleanup policies.
how_to_obtain.command:
# Harbor
curl -s -u admin:$HARBOR_PASS "https://$HARBOR_HOST/api/v2.0/projects/$PROJECT_ID/immutabletagrules" | jq .
curl -s -u admin:$HARBOR_PASS "https://$HARBOR_HOST/api/v2.0/retentions/metadatas" | jq .
# ECR
aws ecr get-lifecycle-policy --repository-name $ECR_REPO_NAME --region $AWS_REGION
# Artifact Registry
gcloud artifacts repositories describe $REPO_NAME --location=$REGION --format=json | jq '.cleanupPolicies'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON response containing at least one retention/lifecycle rule with a defined expiration condition.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For self-hosted distribution/registry, inspect the registry configuration YAML for a storage section. For Harbor, inspect harbor.yml or the database-backed policy exported via API. Retention policies for distribution/registry are handled externally (e.g., cron job scripts), so check for scheduled task definitions.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -A 10 'storage' /etc/docker/registry/config.yml; crontab -l | grep -i 'garbage\|retention\|cleanup'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Either a native retention block exists, or a scheduled cron job invoking 'registry garbage-collect' with a retention script is present.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For ECR, list all repositories and check which ones are missing lifecycle policies to identify gaps.
how_to_obtain.command:
# List repos missing lifecycle policies in ECR
for repo in $(aws ecr describe-repositories --query 'repositories[*].repositoryName' --output text --region $AWS_REGION); do
  policy=$(aws ecr get-lifecycle-policy --repository-name $repo --region $AWS_REGION 2>&1)
  if echo "$policy" | grep -q 'LifecyclePolicyNotFoundException'; then
    echo "MISSING retention policy: $repo"
  fi
done
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No repositories are printed as 'MISSING retention policy'; all repos have at least one lifecycle rule.

typical_values: true (Harbor projects with tag retention rules; ECR repos with lifecycle policies)
false (default for self-hosted distribution/registry with no external GC scripts; new ECR repos before policy is applied)

option_description: Identifies the OS user account under which the registry process or container runs at runtime. This determines the effective UID executing registry operations, managing image storage, and handling client connections. Values range from 'root' (UID 0) to dedicated low-privilege accounts such as 'registry', 'nobody', or a custom non-root user.
security_impact: The Rego rule registry_running_with_excessive_host_privileges fires unconditionally when registry_process_user equals 'root'. Running as root means a process compromise grants an attacker full UID 0 access inside the container, trivially escalating to host takeover when combined with any host volume mount or weak container isolation. This directly enables MITRE T1574.011 (Services Registry Permissions Weakness) and T1547.001 (Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder) exploitation paths.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the running registry container to determine the effective user via docker inspect or by examining the process on the host.
how_to_obtain.command:
# Docker: check User field in container config
docker inspect $(docker ps --filter "name=registry" -q) --format '{{.Config.User}}'
# If empty string returned, process runs as Dockerfile default (check image)
docker inspect $(docker ps --filter "name=registry" -q) --format '{{.Id}}' | xargs -I{} docker exec {} id
# Direct process inspection on host
ps aux | grep -E '[r]egistry' | awk '{print $1}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A non-root username or UID is returned (e.g., 'registry', '1000', 'nobody'). A return of 'root' or UID 0 indicates a finding.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Kubernetes-deployed registries, inspect the pod's security context to determine the effective runAsUser.
how_to_obtain.command:
# Get the pod name for the registry
kubectl get pods -n $NAMESPACE -l app=registry -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}'
# Inspect security context
kubectl get pod $REGISTRY_POD -n $NAMESPACE -o jsonpath='{.spec.securityContext.runAsUser}'
kubectl get pod $REGISTRY_POD -n $NAMESPACE -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[0].securityContext.runAsUser}'
# Exec into pod to verify effective user
kubectl exec -n $NAMESPACE $REGISTRY_POD -- id
how_to_obtain.expected_output: securityContext.runAsUser is set to a non-zero UID, and 'id' inside the pod returns a non-root user.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the Dockerfile for the registry image to find the USER directive, which determines the default process user if not overridden at runtime.
how_to_obtain.command:
# Extract and inspect the image layers to find USER directive
docker history --no-trunc $(docker inspect $(docker ps --filter "name=registry" -q) --format '{{.Image}}') | grep -i 'user'
# Or pull and inspect the Dockerfile if available in the image labels
docker inspect $(docker ps --filter "name=registry" -q) --format '{{index .Config.Labels "maintainer"}}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: USER directive is set to a non-root account (e.g., 'USER registry' or 'USER 1000').

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Harbor deployed via Helm/Kubernetes, check the Helm values file for the securityContext configuration, or inspect it in the cluster via the Kubernetes dashboard.
how_to_obtain.command: helm get values harbor -n $HARBOR_NAMESPACE | grep -A5 'securityContext'
how_to_obtain.navigation: Kubernetes Dashboard → Workloads → Pods → [registry pod] → Spec → Security Context
how_to_obtain.expected_output: runAsUser is set to a non-zero value such as 10000 (Harbor default) or another non-root UID.

typical_values: root (default for many self-hosted distribution/registry Docker images if USER is not explicitly set)
registry (common dedicated service account for hardened deployments)
nobody (minimal privilege account used in some minimalist base images)

option_description: Controls whether the registry container is launched with the Docker or Kubernetes privileged flag set to true. Privileged mode grants the container all Linux capabilities (equivalent to CAP_ALL), disables seccomp and AppArmor profiles, and mounts the host's /dev filesystem, effectively removing container isolation boundaries between the registry process and the host kernel.
security_impact: The Rego rule registry_running_with_excessive_host_privileges fires unconditionally when privileged_mode_enabled is true. A privileged container compromise gives an attacker complete host access — they can mount host filesystems, manipulate kernel parameters, access all block devices, and escape the container entirely. This directly enables supply-chain poisoning (T1525), host persistence (T1547.001), and full host takeover, dramatically increasing the blast radius of any registry vulnerability or misconfiguration.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the running registry container's HostConfig to check the Privileged flag via docker inspect.
how_to_obtain.command:
# Check Privileged field - returns true/false
docker inspect $(docker ps --filter "name=registry" -q) --format '{{.HostConfig.Privileged}}'
# Also check via full JSON for verification
docker inspect $(docker ps --filter "name=registry" -q) | jq '.[0].HostConfig.Privileged'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Returns 'false'. Any return of 'true' indicates the registry is running in fully privileged mode and is a critical finding.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Kubernetes-deployed registries, inspect the pod spec's securityContext for the privileged field on each container.
how_to_obtain.command:
# Check pod-level and container-level privileged setting
kubectl get pod $REGISTRY_POD -n $NAMESPACE -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[*].securityContext.privileged}'
# Full security context dump
kubectl get pod $REGISTRY_POD -n $NAMESPACE -o json | jq '.spec.containers[].securityContext'
# Check all registry pods in namespace
kubectl get pods -n $NAMESPACE -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.metadata.labels.app=="registry") | .spec.containers[].securityContext.privileged'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: All values return 'false' or 'null' (null means not set, defaulting to false). Any 'true' is a critical finding.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the Docker Compose file or Kubernetes manifest used to deploy the registry for the privileged setting.
how_to_obtain.command:
# Docker Compose
grep -n 'privileged' /path/to/docker-compose.yml
# Kubernetes manifest
grep -n 'privileged' /path/to/registry-deployment.yaml
# Helm chart values
helm get values $RELEASE_NAME -n $NAMESPACE | grep -i 'privileged'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: The 'privileged' key is either absent or explicitly set to 'false' in the deployment manifest.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Harbor or other Kubernetes-deployed registries, inspect the pod security context via the Kubernetes dashboard or cloud provider console (e.g., EKS, GKE).
how_to_obtain.navigation: Kubernetes Dashboard → Workloads → Deployments → [registry deployment] → Edit → spec.template.spec.containers[].securityContext.privileged | AWS EKS Console → Clusters → [cluster] → Workloads → [registry pod] → JSON
how_to_obtain.expected_output: privileged field is absent or set to false in the pod spec.

typical_values: false (correct default for all production registry deployments)
true (observed in development environments or misconfigured CI runners where the registry container was granted elevated access for convenience)

option_description: Enumerates the list of host filesystem paths that have been bind-mounted into the registry container at runtime. This includes paths mounted for data persistence (e.g., /data, /var/lib/registry), Docker socket access (/var/run/docker.sock), host configuration directories (/etc), and any other host paths exposed to the container process.
security_impact: The Rego rule registry_running_with_excessive_host_privileges fires when '/var/run/docker.sock' or '/etc' appears in this list. Mounting /var/run/docker.sock inside the registry container grants it full Docker daemon control, enabling an attacker to launch arbitrary privileged containers, read secrets from other containers, or escape to the host. Mounting /etc exposes host authentication files (passwd, shadow, sudoers), SSH keys, and system configuration. Other sensitive mounts like /proc or /sys similarly expand the attack surface to full host compromise via T1574.011.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Enumerate all bind mounts on the running registry container using docker inspect to extract the Mounts array.
how_to_obtain.command:
# List all mounts with type, source, and destination
docker inspect $(docker ps --filter "name=registry" -q) --format '{{json .Mounts}}' | jq '.[] | {Type:.Type, Source:.Source, Destination:.Destination}'
# Quick check specifically for high-risk mounts
docker inspect $(docker ps --filter "name=registry" -q) | jq '.[0].Mounts[] | select(.Source | test("/var/run/docker.sock|/etc|/proc|/sys|/root"))'
# HostConfig Binds array (shows original bind-mount specifications)
docker inspect $(docker ps --filter "name=registry" -q) --format '{{.HostConfig.Binds}}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Only expected data directories (e.g., /var/lib/registry:/var/lib/registry) appear. No /var/run/docker.sock, /etc, /proc, /sys, or other sensitive host paths.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Kubernetes-deployed registries, inspect the pod spec volumes and volumeMounts arrays to identify hostPath volumes.
how_to_obtain.command:
# List all hostPath volumes in the registry pod
kubectl get pod $REGISTRY_POD -n $NAMESPACE -o json | jq '.spec.volumes[] | select(.hostPath != null) | {name:.name, path:.hostPath.path}'
# Cross-reference with container volumeMounts
kubectl get pod $REGISTRY_POD -n $NAMESPACE -o json | jq '.spec.containers[].volumeMounts[] | {name:.name, mountPath:.mountPath}'
# Check all pods labeled as registry in namespace
kubectl get pods -n $NAMESPACE -l app=registry -o json | jq '.items[].spec.volumes[] | select(.hostPath != null)'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No hostPath volumes pointing to /var/run/docker.sock, /etc, /proc, /sys, or other sensitive host directories.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the deployment manifests, Docker Compose files, or Helm chart values for volume mount definitions.
how_to_obtain.command:
# Docker Compose: find all volume definitions
grep -A2 'volumes:' /path/to/docker-compose.yml
# Kubernetes deployment manifest
grep -A5 'hostPath' /path/to/registry-deployment.yaml
grep -B2 'hostPath' /path/to/registry-deployment.yaml
# Helm rendered manifest
helm template $RELEASE_NAME $CHART_PATH -n $NAMESPACE | grep -A3 'hostPath'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: hostPath entries, if present, point only to approved non-sensitive data directories with no system-level host paths.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the team responsible for registry deployment to document why specific host mounts exist, whether they were intentional, and whether alternatives (named volumes, PVCs) were considered for data paths.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: All host mounts have documented justifications. Data persistence uses named volumes or PersistentVolumeClaims rather than bind mounts to host system directories.

typical_values: ['/var/lib/registry'] (standard data directory mount for self-hosted distribution/registry)
['/data/registry', '/certs'] (common production mounts for data and TLS certificates)
['/var/run/docker.sock', '/data'] (misconfigured deployment with unnecessary Docker socket access)
[] (managed registries like ECR, GCR, ACR with no host mounts)

option_description: Lists the Linux capabilities explicitly granted to the registry container beyond the default Docker/container runtime capability set. Added capabilities extend the container's kernel-level privileges in specific dimensions — for example, SYS_ADMIN enables a wide range of system administration operations, NET_ADMIN controls network interfaces and routing, and DAC_OVERRIDE bypasses filesystem permission checks. These are added via Docker's --cap-add flag or Kubernetes securityContext.capabilities.add.
security_impact: The Rego rule registry_running_with_excessive_host_privileges fires when SYS_ADMIN, NET_ADMIN, or DAC_OVERRIDE appears in this list. SYS_ADMIN is nearly equivalent to full root access and enables mounting filesystems, modifying kernel parameters, and container escapes. NET_ADMIN allows traffic interception and network manipulation. DAC_OVERRIDE allows reading and writing any file regardless of permissions, enabling secret exfiltration from any host path. These directly enable T1574.011 (Services Registry Permissions Weakness) and T1547.001 exploitation paths.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the running registry container's HostConfig.CapAdd field via docker inspect to enumerate explicitly added capabilities.
how_to_obtain.command:
# List explicitly added capabilities
docker inspect $(docker ps --filter "name=registry" -q) --format '{{.HostConfig.CapAdd}}'
# Full capability analysis including effective capabilities
docker inspect $(docker ps --filter "name=registry" -q) | jq '.[0].HostConfig | {CapAdd:.CapAdd, CapDrop:.CapDrop}'
# Verify effective capabilities of the registry process on the host
REGISTRY_PID=$(docker inspect --format '{{.State.Pid}}' $(docker ps --filter "name=registry" -q))
cat /proc/$REGISTRY_PID/status | grep -E '^Cap'
# Decode capability bitmask
capsh --decode=$(cat /proc/$REGISTRY_PID/status | grep CapEff | awk '{print $2}')
how_to_obtain.expected_output: CapAdd is null or an empty array. Decoded effective capabilities show only the minimal Docker default set (no SYS_ADMIN, NET_ADMIN, DAC_OVERRIDE, etc.).

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Kubernetes-deployed registries, inspect the pod spec securityContext capabilities section.
how_to_obtain.command:
# Get capabilities added to registry container
kubectl get pod $REGISTRY_POD -n $NAMESPACE -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[0].securityContext.capabilities.add}'
# Full security context including all containers
kubectl get pod $REGISTRY_POD -n $NAMESPACE -o json | jq '.spec.containers[] | {name:.name, capAdd:.securityContext.capabilities.add, capDrop:.securityContext.capabilities.drop}'
# Check for all registry pods
kubectl get pods -n $NAMESPACE -l app=registry -o json | jq '.items[].spec.containers[].securityContext.capabilities'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: capabilities.add is null or empty array. capabilities.drop should ideally contain 'ALL' with only required capabilities re-added.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review Kubernetes deployment manifests and Docker Compose files for cap_add directives or capabilities.add entries.
how_to_obtain.command:
# Docker Compose
grep -A5 'cap_add' /path/to/docker-compose.yml
# Kubernetes manifest
grep -B2 -A10 'capabilities:' /path/to/registry-deployment.yaml
# Check for SYS_ADMIN specifically across all manifests
grep -r 'SYS_ADMIN\|NET_ADMIN\|DAC_OVERRIDE\|SYS_PTRACE' /path/to/k8s-manifests/
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No dangerous capabilities (SYS_ADMIN, NET_ADMIN, DAC_OVERRIDE) are added. Ideally shows capabilities.drop: [ALL] with only NET_BIND_SERVICE re-added if port 443/80 is needed.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the container security policy (PSP, OPA Gatekeeper, Kyverno) enforced on the cluster namespace where the registry runs to verify that added capabilities are restricted by policy.
how_to_obtain.command:
# Check Kyverno policies restricting capabilities
kubectl get clusterpolicies -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.spec.rules[].validate.pattern.spec.containers[].securityContext.capabilities != null)'
# Check OPA/Gatekeeper constraints
kubectl get constraint -A | grep -i 'capability\|privilege'
# Check Pod Security Admission labels on namespace
kubectl get namespace $NAMESPACE -o jsonpath='{.metadata.labels}' | jq .
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A policy is enforced that restricts or denies addition of SYS_ADMIN, NET_ADMIN, and DAC_OVERRIDE capabilities. Namespace is labeled with baseline or restricted pod security standard.

typical_values: [] (correct default — no capabilities added beyond Docker defaults)
['NET_BIND_SERVICE'] (acceptable addition for registries listening on ports below 1024)
['SYS_ADMIN'] (highly dangerous finding observed in misconfigured self-hosted deployments)
['DAC_OVERRIDE', 'CHOWN'] (observed in registries with storage permission workarounds)

option_description: A boolean indicator that reflects whether the currently deployed version of the registry software (identified by registry_software_version) is associated with one or more publicly disclosed CVEs in the National Vulnerability Database (NVD), vendor security advisories, or the Open Source Vulnerability (OSV) database. This must be actively assessed by cross-referencing the version string against vulnerability databases.
security_impact: The Rego rule unpatched_registry_software fires unconditionally when version_has_known_cve is true, regardless of days_since_last_patch. Known CVEs in registry software have included critical vulnerabilities such as authentication bypass (CVE-2022-31690 in Spring-based registries), path traversal enabling arbitrary layer extraction (historical distribution/registry CVEs), and Harbor-specific issues like CVE-2022-31671 (unauthorized access to system info). These map directly to T1190 (Exploit Public-Facing Application) and T1068 (Exploitation for Privilege Escalation), making this a high-severity trigger.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the NVD API and OSV API programmatically to check for CVEs associated with the specific registry software version.
how_to_obtain.command:
# Query NVD API for Harbor CVEs (replace with actual version)
REGISTRY_VERSION="2.9.1"
curl -s "https://services.nvd.nist.gov/rest/json/cves/2.0?keywordSearch=Harbor+$REGISTRY_VERSION&resultsPerPage=20" | jq '.vulnerabilities[].cve | {id:.id, severity:.metrics.cvssMetricV31[0].cvssData.baseSeverity, description:.descriptions[0].value}'
# Query OSV for distribution/registry
curl -s -X POST "https://api.osv.dev/v1/query" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"version":"2.8.3","package":{"name":"github.com/distribution/distribution","ecosystem":"Go"}}' | jq '.vulns[] | {id:.id, summary:.summary}'
# Query for Harbor via OSV
curl -s -X POST "https://api.osv.dev/v1/query" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"version":"2.9.1","package":{"name":"harbor","ecosystem":"Go"}}' | jq '.vulns[].id'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Empty 'vulns' array from OSV and 0 results from NVD indicates no known CVEs. Any returned CVE IDs indicate version_has_known_cve should be set to true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Manually search NVD and vendor security advisories using the registry software name and version string.
how_to_obtain.navigation: NVD Search: https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/search → enter 'Harbor 2.9.1' or 'docker distribution registry 2.8.3' | Harbor Advisories: https://github.com/goharbor/harbor/security/advisories | Quay Advisories: https://access.redhat.com/security/security-updates/ | Nexus Advisories: https://support.sonatype.com/hc/en-us/sections/203012668
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No advisories or CVE entries exist for the specific version. If CVEs appear, note their IDs, CVSS scores, and whether patches are available.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use trivy or grype to scan the registry container image itself for known CVEs, which covers both the registry software and its dependencies.
how_to_obtain.command:
# Trivy scan of the registry container image
REGISTRY_IMAGE=$(docker inspect $(docker ps --filter "name=registry" -q) --format '{{.Config.Image}}')
trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL $REGISTRY_IMAGE
# Grype scan
grype $REGISTRY_IMAGE --fail-on high
# For Harbor specifically
trivy image goharbor/harbor-core:$HARBOR_VERSION --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --format json | jq '.Results[].Vulnerabilities | length'
# Save full report
trivy image $REGISTRY_IMAGE -f json -o /tmp/registry-cve-report.json
cat /tmp/registry-cve-report.json | jq '[.Results[].Vulnerabilities // [] | .[]] | length'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Zero HIGH or CRITICAL CVEs found. Any findings indicate version_has_known_cve should be set to true, with the specific CVE IDs documented.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the organization's vulnerability management platform (Qualys, Tenable, Wiz, Prisma Cloud) for any existing scan results targeting the registry host or container image.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Vulnerability management platform shows no open CVEs for the registry software version, or documents all CVEs as accepted risks with compensating controls.

typical_values: false (current patched versions of Harbor, distribution/registry, Quay with no outstanding CVEs)
true (older Harbor versions: v2.6.x has CVE-2022-31671; distribution/registry v2.7.x has historical CVEs; Nexus versions before 3.41 have known CVEs)

option_description: An integer representing the number of calendar days elapsed since the registry software was last updated to a version that includes a vendor security fix. This is calculated from the release date of the currently deployed version as published in the vendor's changelog or GitHub releases page. If the registry has never been updated since initial deployment, the value reflects days since initial deployment. Valid range is 0–3650 days.
security_impact: The Rego rule unpatched_registry_software fires when days_since_last_patch exceeds 90 days, operating independently of version_has_known_cve. A registry not updated within 90 days may be missing multiple rounds of security patches addressing newly disclosed vulnerabilities. Container registry software is a high-value target — historical security patches have addressed critical issues including authentication bypass, SSRF, and privilege escalation. Stale versions increase exposure to T1190 (Exploit Public-Facing Application) and T1068 (Exploitation for Privilege Escalation) even before specific CVEs are published, as attackers exploit patch deltas between versions.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Retrieve the release date of the currently deployed version from the vendor's GitHub releases API or changelog to compute patch age.
how_to_obtain.command:
# Harbor: get release date from GitHub
HARBOR_VERSION="v2.9.1"
curl -s "https://api.github.com/repos/goharbor/harbor/releases/tags/$HARBOR_VERSION" | jq '{tag_name:.tag_name, published_at:.published_at}'
# Distribution/registry release date
REGISTRY_VERSION="v2.8.3"
curl -s "https://api.github.com/repos/distribution/distribution/releases/tags/$REGISTRY_VERSION" | jq '{tag_name:.tag_name, published_at:.published_at}'
# Compute days since release (requires the release date from above)
RELEASE_DATE="2023-11-15"
echo $(( ($(date +%s) - $(date -d "$RELEASE_DATE" +%s)) / 86400 )) days since release
# Quay
curl -s "https://api.github.com/repos/quay/quay/releases/tags/$QUAY_VERSION" | jq '.published_at'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Release date is retrieved; computed days since that release is less than 90. Values over 90 days trigger the unpatched_registry_software rule.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check the vendor's release notes or GitHub releases page to identify the release date of the currently deployed version, then calculate elapsed days.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Harbor Releases: https://github.com/goharbor/harbor/releases | Distribution/Registry Releases: https://github.com/distribution/distribution/releases | Quay Releases: https://github.com/quay/quay/releases | Nexus Release Notes: https://help.sonatype.com/en/sonatype-nexus-repository-release-notes.html | JFrog Release Notes: https://jfrog.com/help/r/jfrog-release-information
how_to_obtain.expected_output: The release date for the deployed version is identified. Subtract from today's date; result should be under 90 days for a compliant deployment.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check the container image creation date as a proxy for when the registry software was last updated, then cross-reference with vendor release notes.
how_to_obtain.command:
# Get image creation date from container metadata
docker inspect $(docker ps --filter "name=registry" -q) --format '{{.Created}}'
# Get image build date from OCI labels
docker inspect $(docker ps --filter "name=registry" -q) | jq '.[0].Config.Labels["org.opencontainers.image.created"]'
# For Kubernetes: get image creation date
kubectl get pod $REGISTRY_POD -n $NAMESPACE -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[0].image}' | xargs docker inspect 2>/dev/null | jq '.[0].Created'
# Calculate days since image creation (approximate for patch age)
IMAGE_DATE=$(docker inspect $(docker ps --filter "name=registry" -q) | jq -r '.[0].Created')
echo $(( ($(date +%s) - $(date -d "$IMAGE_DATE" +%s)) / 86400 )) days since image was built
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Image creation date is recent (within 90 days). Note: image creation date is only a proxy — verify against vendor release notes for the actual security patch date of the deployed version.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the platform/DevOps team responsible for registry maintenance to determine their patch cadence, last update date, and whether automated image update mechanisms (e.g., Renovate, Dependabot, image policy controllers) are in place.
how_to_obtain.command:
# Check for automated update tooling in the repo
find /path/to/infra-repo -name "renovate.json" -o -name ".dependabot.yml" -o -name "*.yaml" | xargs grep -l 'registry\|harbor\|quay' 2>/dev/null
# Check Flux/ArgoCD image automation policies
kubectl get imageupdateautomation -A 2>/dev/null
kubectl get imagepolicy -A 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Team confirms a patch review cycle of 30–90 days maximum, automated tooling is configured to detect new registry versions, and the last update was within 90 days.

typical_values: 0-30 (actively maintained deployments with automated image updates or monthly patch cycles)
91-180 (borderline non-compliant; triggers unpatched_registry_software rule; common in teams without automated patching)
181-365 (high-risk finding common in long-running self-hosted registries with manual maintenance)
365+ (critical finding observed in neglected on-premises registry deployments)

option_description: Controls whether the registry enforces per-client, per-IP, or per-token rate limits on image pull requests to prevent resource exhaustion, bandwidth abuse, and denial-of-service conditions on the registry API and storage backend.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires `missing_pull_rate_limiting_and_abuse_controls` when both `pull_rate_limiting_enabled` and `auth_endpoint_rate_limiting_enabled` are false, or when `anonymous_pull_enabled` is true and `pull_rate_limiting_enabled` is false. Without this control, an attacker can exhaust registry bandwidth and storage I/O, degrading availability for production image pulls, and can enumerate repositories without throttling. The scoring is low (2) but the availability impact on CI/CD pipelines justifies high criticality classification.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For nginx-fronted self-hosted registries, inspect the nginx configuration for limit_req_zone and limit_req directives applied to the registry upstream.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -rE 'limit_req_zone|limit_req|rate=' /etc/nginx/nginx.conf /etc/nginx/conf.d/ /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lines such as 'limit_req_zone $binary_remote_addr zone=registry_pull:10m rate=10r/s;' and 'limit_req zone=registry_pull burst=20 nodelay;' confirm rate limiting is active. No output indicates the control is absent.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Harbor registry, check the rate-limiting middleware configuration in harbor.yml or the Nginx proxy configuration bundled with Harbor.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -A5 -i 'rate' /etc/harbor/harbor.yml 2>/dev/null || docker exec -it nginx cat /etc/nginx/nginx.conf | grep -i limit_req
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Presence of rate-limit keys or limit_req directives confirms enforcement. Harbor does not natively expose a single 'rate limiting' toggle; middleware configuration is the authoritative source.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For cloud-managed registries such as AWS ECR, check for AWS WAF or API Gateway throttling rules associated with the registry endpoint via the AWS CLI.
how_to_obtain.command: aws wafv2 list-web-acls --scope REGIONAL --query 'WebACLs[*].{Name:Name,ARN:ARN}' --output table && aws wafv2 get-web-acl --name <waf-name> --scope REGIONAL --id <waf-id> --query 'WebACL.Rules[*].{Name:Name,Action:Action}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A rule with action 'Block' or 'Count' referencing rate-based statements (RateBasedStatement) targeting the registry domain confirms rate limiting is in place.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Simulate rapid sequential pull requests and observe whether the registry returns HTTP 429 Too Many Requests responses, confirming throttling is active.
how_to_obtain.command: for i in $(seq 1 50); do curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' -u user:pass https://<registry-host>/v2/<repo>/manifests/latest; done | sort | uniq -c
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Presence of HTTP 429 responses in the output confirms rate limiting is enforced. Only 200/401 responses with no 429 indicates the control is absent.

typical_values: true (enforced via nginx or HAProxy in hardened deployments)
true (AWS ECR behind WAF rate-based rules)

option_description: Controls whether the registry authentication service (token server, OAuth proxy, LDAP authenticator, or native /v2/auth endpoint) enforces failed-attempt thresholds, temporary IP lockouts, or requests-per-second caps to prevent brute-force credential attacks against registry login.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires `missing_pull_rate_limiting_and_abuse_controls` when both `pull_rate_limiting_enabled` and `auth_endpoint_rate_limiting_enabled` are false simultaneously. Without auth endpoint rate limiting, an attacker can perform unlimited brute-force attempts against registry credentials (T1110) using automated tooling against the /v2/auth or token issuance endpoint without any throttling or account lockout, eventually obtaining valid credentials to pull sensitive images or push malicious ones.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Harbor with its built-in token service, check the nginx configuration that fronts the core service for rate limit directives on the /service/token path.
how_to_obtain.command: docker exec -it nginx grep -A10 'location.*service/token\|location.*v2/auth' /etc/nginx/nginx.conf
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output containing 'limit_req zone=' applied to the auth location block confirms rate limiting on the authentication endpoint. No directive indicates the control is absent.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For an OAuth2 proxy (e.g., oauth2-proxy) fronting the registry auth service, inspect its configuration for rate-limiting options or check the upstream identity provider (Keycloak, Okta) for brute-force protection settings.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -iE 'brute.force|rate.limit|max.attempts|lockout|fail2ban' /etc/oauth2-proxy/oauth2-proxy.cfg /etc/keycloak/standalone/configuration/standalone.xml 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Configuration keys referencing attempt limits or lockout durations confirm the control is active. Empty output indicates reliance on default (typically unlimited) behavior.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Harbor web UI, navigate to Administration > Configuration > Auth and check if any LDAP or OIDC provider is configured. Then validate brute-force protection at the identity provider level (e.g., Keycloak Realm Settings > Security Defenses > Brute Force Detection).
how_to_obtain.navigation: Harbor UI: Administration > Configuration > Authentication | Keycloak Admin Console: Realm Settings > Security Defenses > Brute Force Detection > Enable Brute Force Detection = ON
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Keycloak shows 'Brute Force Detection: Enabled' with non-zero values for Max Login Failures and Wait Increment. Harbor itself defers auth rate limiting to the identity provider or the nginx proxy layer.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Send repeated failed authentication requests to the /v2/auth endpoint and observe whether HTTP 429 or temporary 401 lockout responses appear after a threshold.
how_to_obtain.command: for i in $(seq 1 20); do curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' 'https://<registry-host>/v2/auth?service=<service>&scope=repository:test:pull' -u testuser:wrongpassword; sleep 0.1; done | sort | uniq -c
how_to_obtain.expected_output: HTTP 429 responses or progressively delayed 401 responses after several attempts confirm lockout or rate limiting is active. Consistent rapid 401 responses with no throttling confirm the control is absent.

typical_values: false (default for Docker Distribution token server)
true (enforced via nginx rate limiting on /v2/auth)
true (enforced by upstream IdP brute-force protection in enterprise deployments)
